source.title: Task Competence Is Not Instruction Following: Evaluating Instruction-Conflicting Behavior in Small Language Models

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: Measures task accuracy across model sizes, bearing on downstream performance versus scale (V6), but does not measure the original studies’ held-out loss or fit their scaling-law method.
record.gate_note: Only standard-instruction task accuracy across model sizes bears on V6. The paper’s non-standard accuracy and IFFR concern instruction-conflicting behavior, not any listed claim version. It does not report held-out cross-entropy, training-token or compute sweeps, extrapolation from fitted losses, compute-optimal allocations, or architecture comparisons. Prompt instructions shown in the paper are experimental examples, not instructions addressed to an AI reviewing the text.
record.test_reason: The study is about instruction following, not scaling laws. Its standard-instruction accuracy for five Qwen3.5 instruction-tuned sizes (0.8B–27B) on nine datasets is still a result on V6, measured in a new setting: post-trained checkpoints, zero-shot closed-set or numeric scoring. It fits no scaling relation and measures no pretraining loss, so it bears only on whether accuracy rises with size, not on whether it does so predictably.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Their main conclusion is that task competence and instruction following are distinct abilities. Small models solve tasks but ignore conflicting instructions; larger models follow them more reliably, so scale narrows the gap. They note that standard accuracy and instruction following both 'generally improve with scale' but inconsistently across tasks and datasets. They make no claim about predictable or fitted scaling.
record.recipe_differences: Evaluates standard task accuracy on instruction-tuned checkpoints at five sizes; it does not reproduce held-out cross-entropy measurements or fit parameter-, token-, or compute-scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and task change the standard-accuracy trend; the paper reports some non-monotonic steps. Prompt-variant means and standard deviations are reported, but prompt-variant effects concern instruction-following results rather than the claim’s loss-scaling measures.

fits_no_version.finding: Following conflicting (non-standard) instructions improves with model size: IFFR drops from 70–98% at 0.8B to roughly 0.5–9% at 27B on most datasets. It is non-monotonic on MultiArith (IFFR rises to 17.73 at 27B) and on Rotten Tomatoes and FinancialPhraseBank at 9B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Instruction-following ability under instructions that conflict with a learned task prior improves with model scale, separately from task accuracy.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 3rd Workshop on Language Understanding in the Human-Machine Era (LUHME 2026)
record.problems: Only one model family and five checkpoints are evaluated. The paper reports downstream accuracy, not held-out loss, and does not fit or validate predictions from a scaling law. Results vary by task and dataset. The 9B and 27B API backend precision was not directly controlled.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant standard-accuracy rows left out. Non-standard accuracy and IFFR results in Tables 3–8 and Figures 3–4 were omitted because they measure instruction-conflicting behavior, not the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss and no parameter, token or compute sweeps.
No fitted laws and no extrapolation to larger runs.
No architecture or shape comparisons at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities, repeated-data, or fine-tuning/transfer scaling laws.
No fitted or predictive relation between accuracy and size; no link to pretraining loss; no extrapolation test. Only five sizes in one instruction-tuned family were evaluated.
No fitted exponents or comparisons across fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The study is evidence on V6 only incidentally, with five points per dataset. Confound: for sentiment and math, the 0.8B–4B models ran locally in fp16 while the 9B and 27B ran through the DeepInfra API at uncontrolled precision. The 4B→9B step therefore also changes backend, which may affect the 9B dips (r19, r29, r39). Tables 3–5 duplicate the means in Tables 6–8. Several sentiment datasets are near ceiling, which limits what they can show about scaling.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or parameter/token/compute loss scaling is measured.
No small-run loss fits or larger-run loss predictions are evaluated.
No fixed-compute allocation between parameters and tokens is evaluated.
No depth, width, or other architecture comparison at fixed parameter count is reported.
No other modality, repeated-data, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling-law test is reported.

Measures standard task accuracy across five sizes in one instruction-tuned model family, but does not fit a predictive scaling relationship, test extrapolation, or relate performance to pretraining loss.
No fitted loss exponents or compute-optimal allocation are compared across fitting choices or setups.

relationships.condition: RACE-Middle, ARC-Challenge, OpenBookQA-Main, Rotten Tomatoes and MAWPS, Qwen3.5 0.8B–27B instruction-tuned
relationships.reason: Standard accuracy rises at every size step on these datasets, e.g. ARC-C 64.95→97.51 and MAWPS 27.04→93.61 (r2–r5, r7–r10, r12–r15, r22–r25, r32–r35).
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy increased at every size step on all five datasets, including ARC-Challenge gains from 64.95 to 97.51 and MAWPS gains from 27.04 to 93.61.

relationships.reason: Accuracy is flat or non-monotonic across a 30x size range. Multi-class Sentiment moves only 88.08→90.24, and FinancialPhraseBank dips at 4B/9B before 99.49 at 27B (r17–r20, r27–r30).
relationships.display_finding: Across a 30× size range, Multi-class Sentiment changed only 88.08→90.24, while FinancialPhraseBank dipped at 4B and 9B before reaching 99.49 at 27B.

relationships.reason: Gains are not smooth. MultiArith stays at floor through 2B, then jumps to 48.33 at 4B (r42, r43). Calc-asdiv-a dips at 9B with large prompt variance (r39). Downstream gains here are not readily predictable from size.
relationships.display_finding: MultiArith stayed at floor through 2B before jumping to 48.33 at 4B, while Calc-asdiv-a dipped at 9B with substantial prompt variance.
